description: Verdikt accuracy benchmark — curated disputes with a defensible 'correct' verdict a fair human arbitrator would reach. Fired through the hardened 3-label prompt (InjectionProbe) and scored on agreement with `expected` and on byte-identical panel convergence. SPLIT cases are inherently the most debatable; treat per-outcome accuracy accordingly.

cases.evidence: Buyer ordered a laptop and paid in full. The seller never shipped it: courier records show no shipping label was ever created and nothing was dispatched. Thirty days have passed with no delivery and the seller has stopped responding to messages.

Buyer paid a freelancer for a market report due in seven days. By the deadline the freelancer had delivered nothing, and admitted in writing that they never started the work and could not complete it.
Buyer purchased event tickets. The seller sent confirmation screenshots, but the venue's official records confirm no tickets were ever issued to the buyer and the screenshots were fabricated.

Seller's listing promised a 'new, fully functional' appliance. Photos taken on delivery show it arrived cracked and not powering on. The seller acknowledges it was damaged in transit but refuses any remedy.

Seller shipped the item; the courier shows it delivered and signed for at the buyer's registered address on time. The item matches the listing photos and description exactly. The buyer admits they simply changed their mind after it arrived.

A freelancer delivered the agreed website on the due date, matching the signed specification. The client accepted it and deployed it to production, then opened a dispute requesting a full refund without citing any defect or unmet requirement.

Seller granted access to a digital course immediately upon purchase. Platform logs show the buyer completed 90% of the lessons over three weeks before requesting a full refund, citing no problem with the content.

The buyer claims the package never arrived. The seller provides a courier-signed delivery receipt and a timestamped doorbell-camera clip showing the package handed directly to the buyer at their door.

The seller shipped the correct item, but it arrived ten days late, after the event the buyer needed it for. The item itself is exactly as described and is fully usable for other purposes. Both the delay (seller) and the still-usable goods (value to buyer) are undisputed.

A freelancer was hired for a logo plus social-media templates and an icon set. They delivered the logo and brand palette, which the client accepted and is using commercially, but never delivered the templates or icons. Roughly half the agreed deliverables are outstanding.

Buyer ordered ten identical units. The seller delivered six in good condition and on time; the remaining four were never shipped. The buyer kept and is using the six delivered units but is demanding a full refund of the entire order.

Both sides share fault. The seller's sizing instructions were ambiguous, which led to a wrong-size order; the buyer also ignored a clarification email from the seller before completing the purchase. The item is unused and in resellable condition.
